title: The Hasideans
lead: A group of devout Jews, "mighty warriors of Israel" devoted to the law, who joined the Maccabean revolt (1 Maccabees 2:42) and were the first to make peace with the high priest Alcimus, who then killed sixty of them (1 Maccabees 7:12–18). Their name is the Greek form of the Hebrew hasidim, "the loyal" or "the pious". Who they were, and whether later groups grew out of them, is much debated.

sections.h: In the books of the Maccabees
sections.b: 1 Maccabees names the Hasideans twice. They join Mattathias as "a company of Hasideans... each one ready to give himself for the law" (1 Maccabees 2:42). Later, when Alcimus comes as high priest with the Seleucid army, they are "the first among the Israelites to seek peace", trusting that "a priest of the line of Aaron" will do them no wrong. He kills sixty of them in one day, and the writer quotes Psalm 79 over them (1 Maccabees 7:13–17). 2 Maccabees puts a different charge in Alcimus's mouth: that the Hasideans, led by Judas, keep the war going (2 Maccabees 14:6).

In the psalms, God's hasidim are his faithful people, those bound to him by covenant love (hesed): "Bring together to me those loyal to me" (Psalm 50:5). 1 Maccabees 7:17 quotes Psalm 79:2–3, where the same word stands for those whose blood was poured out around Jerusalem. Whether the Hasideans were a defined party with leaders, or simply a name for the devout, the texts do not say.

Older scholarship often made the Hasideans the parent group of both the Pharisees and the Essenes, and linked them with the "wise" of Daniel 11:33–35 and the "little help" of Daniel 11:34. Many recent scholars doubt this. The sources are few, and nothing shows that the Hasideans were a single organized sect. The medieval and modern Hasidic movements took the same Hebrew word, but have no historical link with them.
